reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder of the Navajo (Diné) population caused by a founder mutation in MPV17, producing a hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome
Combines progressive liver disease with a severe sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy and central white-matter involvement (leukoencephalopathy)
Neuropathy leads to distal weakness, sensory loss, painless injuries, acral mutilation, and corneal anaesthesia with recurrent ulceration
Hepatic presentations range from infantile liver failure to a slowly progressive childhood cirrhosis
Metabolic decompensation may be accompanied by lactic acidosis reflecting impaired oxidative phosphorylation
Diagnosis rests on the ethnic background, characteristic neurological and hepatic features, quantitative mitochondrial DNA depletion in liver, and MPV17 sequencing
Management is supportive; liver transplantation may be considered for hepatic failure but does not arrest the progressive neurological disease
reference.pathophysiology: Navajo neurohepatopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in MPV17, which encodes an inner mitochondrial membrane protein needed to maintain the deoxyribonucleotide pool and mitochondrial DNA. Loss of function leads to depletion of mitochondrial DNA in the liver and nervous system, impairing oxidative phosphorylation in tissues with high energy demand. The result is progressive hepatocellular injury alongside a demyelinating/axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and leukoencephalopathy, with lactic acidosis during metabolic stress. A founder MPV17 variant underlies the disorder in the Navajo population.
additionalDifferentials: Other hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes (DGUOK, POLG, MPV17-related non-Navajo)
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests, serum bile acids, and lactate/pyruvate
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography documenting sensorimotor neuropathy
Liver biopsy with quantitative mitochondrial DNA content showing depletion
Respiratory chain enzyme analysis in liver or muscle
redFlags: Acute infantile liver failure with coagulopathy and lactic acidosis
Corneal anaesthesia leading to unnoticed ulceration and visual loss
Progressive acral mutilation from sensory loss and painless injury
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is poor: the infantile hepatic form may cause early liver failure and death, and even in the more slowly progressive childhood form the neurological disability advances relentlessly; liver transplantation does not correct the neuropathy or leukoencephalopathy.
pitfalls: Attributing painless injuries or mutilation to non-accidental causes rather than a sensory neuropathy
Expecting liver transplantation to halt neurological progression
Missing corneal anaesthesia and failing to protect the eye
Overlooking mitochondrial disease when liver dysfunction and neuropathy coexist
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Suchy, Sokol & Balistreri, Liver Disease in Children
management: No disease-specific therapy exists, so care is supportive, with nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and management of coagulopathy in chronic liver disease
Avoidance of hepatotoxic agents and prompt treatment of intercurrent illness, with correction of lactic acidosis during metabolic decompensation
Consideration of liver transplantation for hepatic failure, recognising it does not halt the neuropathy or leukoencephalopathy
Protective care of insensate limbs with meticulous foot and wound care to prevent painless injury and acral mutilation
Ophthalmic lubrication and corneal protection to prevent ulceration from corneal anaesthesia
Multidisciplinary input from hepatology, neurology and ophthalmology, with physiotherapy and orthoses for neuropathic weakness
Genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal recessive MPV17 founder mutation
